questions.title: Venous openings into the right atrium
questions.question: The superior and inferior venae cavae open into which part of the right atrium?

options.A: The rough atrium proper, anterior to the crista terminalis
options.B: The smooth-walled sinus venarum, posterior to the crista terminalis
options.D: The atrial septum, directly into the fossa ovalis

explanations.A: Incorrect. The rough atrium proper, lined by pectinate muscles, lies anterior to the crista terminalis and receives the right auricle, not the two venae cavae.
explanations.B: Correct. The crista terminalis, a muscular ridge, divides the right atrium into an anterior, rough-walled atrium proper (derived embryologically from the primitive atrium and lined by pectinate muscles) and a posterior, smooth-walled sinus venarum (derived from the absorbed sinus venosus); the superior vena cava opens into the upper part of the sinus venarum and the inferior vena cava into its lower part, the latter guarded by a vestigial valve. This smooth-versus-rough distinction, with both great veins opening into the smooth part, is exactly what the practical bank's labelled images of the right atrium's interior test. Locating the venous openings in the smooth sinus venarum rather than the rough, pectinate-muscle-lined atrium proper is the discrimination this item tests.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The right auricle is a small conical pouch projecting from the rough atrium proper; the venae cavae do not open into it.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The fossa ovalis is a depression on the atrial septum, the remnant of the foramen ovale, a separate structure from either venous opening.

questions.subject: cvs
questions.learning_objective: State that the superior and inferior venae cavae open into the smooth-walled sinus venarum of the right atrium.

questions.title: Contents of the anterior interventricular groove
questions.question: Which two vessels run together in the anterior interventricular groove of the heart?

options.A: The right coronary artery and the small cardiac vein
options.B: The anterior interventricular (left anterior descending) artery and the great cardiac vein
options.C: The circumflex artery and the coronary sinus
options.D: The posterior interventricular artery and the middle cardiac vein

explanations.A: Incorrect. The right coronary artery runs the coronary sulcus, not the anterior interventricular groove, and the small cardiac vein accompanies it there, not in the anterior interventricular groove.
explanations.B: Correct. The anterior interventricular artery, the left coronary artery's larger terminal branch (commonly the "LAD"), runs down the anterior interventricular groove accompanied by the great cardiac vein, which begins near the apex and ascends alongside it before curving back in the coronary sulcus to become the coronary sinus. Together these two vessels, one arterial and one venous, occupy the same groove and supply/drain much of the anterior interventricular septum and adjacent ventricular walls. Pairing the anterior interventricular artery with the great cardiac vein, rather than the small or middle cardiac veins which lie elsewhere, is the discrimination this item tests.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The circumflex artery runs in the left part of the coronary (atrioventricular) sulcus, not the anterior interventricular groove; the coronary sinus itself lies in the posterior coronary sulcus, receiving the great cardiac vein rather than running alongside the anterior interventricular artery.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The posterior interventricular artery and the middle cardiac vein occupy the POSTERIOR interventricular groove, the mirror-image structure on the diaphragmatic surface of the heart, not the anterior groove.

questions.subject: cvs
questions.learning_objective: Identify the anterior interventricular artery and great cardiac vein as the vessels occupying the anterior interventricular groove.

questions.title: Nerve relations of the arch of the aorta
questions.question: As the left vagus nerve crosses the left side of the arch of the aorta, which branch does it give off there, and what other nerve also lies in close relation to the arch at this point?

options.A: It gives off the left recurrent laryngeal nerve, which hooks beneath the arch beside the ligamentum arteriosum; the left phrenic nerve also crosses the arch's left side, anterior to the vagus
options.B: It gives off the left phrenic nerve, which hooks beneath the arch; the recurrent laryngeal nerve lies posterior to it
options.C: It gives off the external laryngeal nerve, which hooks beneath the arch; the right phrenic nerve lies anterior to it
options.D: It gives no branch at the arch; both the phrenic and recurrent laryngeal nerves cross only the pulmonary trunk, not the aorta

explanations.A: Correct. As the left vagus nerve descends across the left side of the arch of the aorta, it gives off the left recurrent laryngeal nerve, which hooks beneath the arch immediately beside the ligamentum arteriosum before ascending in the tracheo-oesophageal groove to supply the larynx; the left phrenic nerve runs down separately, anterior to the vagus, also crossing the arch's left side on its way to the diaphragm. This shared left-sided relation to the arch, vagus and phrenic both crossing it with the recurrent laryngeal nerve branching off and hooking under it, is exactly why the arch of the aorta is a classic site of injury to both nerves in aortic arch aneurysm or surgery, producing hoarseness and/or a paralysed hemidiaphragm. Distinguishing which nerve hooks under the arch (the recurrent laryngeal) from which merely crosses its surface (the phrenic) is the discrimination this item tests.
explanations.B: Incorrect. It is the recurrent laryngeal nerve, not the phrenic nerve, that hooks beneath the arch; the phrenic nerve instead continues down the arch's surface toward the diaphragm without hooking back.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The vagus gives off the recurrent laryngeal nerve at the arch, not the external laryngeal nerve, which branches much higher, from the vagus in the neck; the phrenic nerve relation described is also the LEFT phrenic nerve, not the right.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Both nerves do relate directly to the arch of the aorta itself, on its left side, the recurrent laryngeal nerve hooking beneath it and the phrenic nerve crossing its surface, not to the pulmonary trunk.

questions.subject: cvs
questions.learning_objective: State the relations of the left vagus, left recurrent laryngeal and left phrenic nerves to the arch of the aorta.

questions.title: Coronary sulcus contents and the conducting system
questions.question: Which vessel runs in the coronary (atrioventricular) sulcus and, in most people, supplies the whole conducting system of the heart?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The circumflex artery, a branch of the LEFT coronary artery, runs the left part of the coronary sulcus and supplies the left atrium and part of the left ventricle; it supplies the conducting system only in the minority of people with left dominance.
explanations.B: Correct. The right coronary artery runs the coronary sulcus between the right atrium and right ventricle, giving off the right marginal artery and, on reaching the posterior/diaphragmatic surface, the posterior interventricular artery; in the majority of people it also supplies the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes, making it the dominant vessel for the heart's conducting system as well as its whole right side. The coronary sinus, the venous counterpart running the posterior part of the same sulcus, drains alongside it but does not itself supply the conducting system. Recognising the right coronary artery, not the circumflex artery or the venous system, as the usual supply to the conducting system is the discrimination this item tests.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The anterior interventricular artery runs the anterior interventricular groove, not the coronary sulcus, and mainly supplies the anterior septum and ventricular walls.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The great cardiac vein is a venous structure that drains, rather than supplies, the heart, and does not itself perfuse the conducting system.

questions.subject: cvs
questions.learning_objective: Identify the right coronary artery as the vessel of the coronary sulcus that usually supplies the heart's conducting system.

questions.title: Origin of the internal thoracic artery
questions.question: The internal thoracic artery arises from which vessel?

options.A: The first part of the subclavian artery
options.C: The second part of the subclavian artery

explanations.A: Correct. The internal thoracic (internal mammary) artery arises from the first part of the subclavian artery, medial to scalenus anterior, alongside the vertebral artery and the thyrocervical trunk, the first part's three named branches. From its origin it descends behind the upper six costal cartilages, about a fingerbreadth from the sternal edge, to end opposite the sixth intercostal space by dividing into the musculophrenic and superior epigastric arteries. Recognising the first part of the subclavian artery, rather than the thyrocervical trunk (a sibling branch of the same part) or a more distal segment, as its true origin is the discrimination this item tests.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The thyrocervical trunk is itself a separate branch of the first part of the subclavian artery, a sibling of the internal thoracic artery, not its parent vessel.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The second part of the subclavian artery, behind scalenus anterior, gives only the costocervical trunk, not the internal thoracic artery.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The axillary artery, the subclavian's continuation beyond the first rib, is far too distal and lateral to be this vessel's origin.

questions.subject: cvs
questions.learning_objective: State that the internal thoracic artery arises from the first part of the subclavian artery.

questions.title: Formation and termination of the superior vena cava
questions.question: The superior vena cava is formed by the union of which two veins, and where does it enter the right atrium?

options.A: The two brachiocephalic veins, uniting behind the first right costal cartilage; it enters the right atrium behind the third right costal cartilage
options.B: The two internal jugular veins, uniting behind the manubrium; it enters the right atrium behind the second right costal cartilage
options.C: The right brachiocephalic vein and the azygos vein, uniting behind the second right costal cartilage; it enters the right atrium behind the fourth right costal cartilage
options.D: The two subclavian veins, uniting behind the sternoclavicular joint; it enters the right atrium behind the first right costal cartilage

explanations.A: Correct. The superior vena cava is formed by the union of the two brachiocephalic veins behind the lower border of the first right costal cartilage; about 5 cm long, it descends to open into the right atrium behind the third right costal cartilage, receiving the azygos vein, its one named tributary, from behind just before it pierces the fibrous pericardium at the second right costal cartilage. Each brachiocephalic vein is itself formed, in the root of the neck, by the union of an internal jugular and a subclavian vein on the same side, a separate, earlier union from the one that forms the SVC itself. Getting the SVC's own formation (two brachiocephalic veins) and termination level (behind the third right costal cartilage) right, distinct from the brachiocephalic veins' own formation further upstream, is the discrimination this item tests.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The two internal jugular veins do not unite to form the SVC; each internal jugular unites with its own side's subclavian vein instead, forming a brachiocephalic vein, one step upstream of the SVC.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The azygos vein is the SVC's tributary, entering it near its termination, not a vessel that unites with the right brachiocephalic vein to form it; the SVC is formed purely by the two brachiocephalic veins.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The two subclavian veins do not unite directly; each subclavian instead unites with its own side's internal jugular vein to form a brachiocephalic vein, which is the vessel that unites with its pair to form the SVC.

questions.subject: cvs
questions.learning_objective: State the union that forms the superior vena cava and the level at which it enters the right atrium.

questions.title: Azygos vein impression on the right lung
questions.question: On the mediastinal surface of the RIGHT lung, which of the following produces a groove or impression?

options.B: The azygos vein, arching over the root of the lung

explanations.A: Incorrect. The arch of the aorta grooves the mediastinal surface of the LEFT lung, not the right.
explanations.B: Correct. The mediastinal surface of the right lung is grooved by structures related to the right side of the mediastinum, chiefly the superior vena cava anteriorly and the azygos vein, which arches over the root of the right lung from behind before draining into the SVC, producing its own impression above the hilum. This right-sided impression pattern (SVC, azygos arch) contrasts with the left lung, whose mediastinal surface is instead grooved by the aortic arch and its great branches. Recognising the azygos vein's impression as a right-lung feature, not a left-lung one, is the discrimination this item tests.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The left brachiocephalic vein lies anterior to the trachea in the superior mediastinum and does not characteristically groove the right lung's mediastinal surface the way the azygos vein does.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The pulmonary trunk contributes to the cardiac impression anteriorly on the left lung, not to a distinct right-lung groove.

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: Identify the azygos vein's impression on the mediastinal surface of the right lung.

questions.title: Tracheal bifurcation level and anterior relations
questions.question: At what level does the trachea bifurcate into the two principal bronchi, and which structure lies immediately anterior to its thoracic part?

options.A: The sternal angle (~T4); the manubrium and left brachiocephalic vein lie anterior
options.B: The suprasternal notch (~T2); the thymus alone lies anterior
options.C: The xiphisternal junction (~T9); the pericardium lies anterior
options.D: The cricoid cartilage (~C6); the thyroid isthmus lies anterior

explanations.A: Correct. The trachea, continuing the larynx from the lower border of C6, descends through the neck and thorax to bifurcate into the two principal bronchi at the sternal angle, roughly the T4 vertebral level; its thoracic part lies with the manubrium and the left brachiocephalic vein anteriorly, the oesophagus and left recurrent laryngeal nerve behind, and the great vessels of the superior mediastinum flanking it on either side. The sternal angle is a useful external landmark precisely because it marks both the tracheal bifurcation internally and the plane separating the superior from the inferior mediastinum. Locating the bifurcation at the sternal angle (T4), with the manubrium and left brachiocephalic vein anterior to the trachea at that level, is the discrimination this item tests.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The suprasternal notch marks roughly where the trachea enters the thorax from the neck, not where it bifurcates; and the manubrium and left brachiocephalic vein, not the thymus alone, lie anterior to the thoracic trachea.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The xiphisternal junction is far too low and marks the inferior end of the sternum, well below the level of tracheal bifurcation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. C6 and the cricoid cartilage mark where the trachea BEGINS, continuing the larynx, not where it bifurcates; the thyroid gland constricts the trachea near its upper end, not at the bifurcation.

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: State the level of the tracheal bifurcation and the structures immediately anterior to the thoracic trachea.

questions.title: The cardiac notch of the left lung
questions.question: The cardiac notch, a deep concavity on the anterior border of the lung that leaves part of the pericardium uncovered, is a feature of which lung?

options.D: Neither lung — it is a feature of the pericardium only

explanations.A: Incorrect. The right lung's anterior border is nearly straight, without a comparable deep notch; the cardiac notch is a left-lung feature.
explanations.B: Correct. The left lung's anterior border carries a deep cardiac notch, which together with the lingula, the left lung's small tongue-shaped projection analogous to the right middle lobe, leaves part of the pericardium and heart uncovered by lung tissue at the front of the chest. The left lung's mediastinal surface, above and behind the cardiac impression, is further grooved by the arch of the aorta and the descending aorta. This left-sided cardiac notch, absent from the right lung's more gently curved anterior border, is the feature this item tests.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The cardiac notch is asymmetric, a left-lung feature only, reflecting the heart's own leftward-shifted position in the thorax.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The cardiac notch is a feature of the lung's own anterior border, specifically the left lung, not of the pericardium.

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: Identify the cardiac notch as a feature of the left lung's anterior border, related to the arch of the aorta impression.

questions.title: Origin and diaphragmatic opening of the oesophagus
questions.question: At what level does the oesophagus begin, continuing from the pharynx, and where does it leave the thorax through the diaphragm?

options.A: Begins at C6 (lower border of the cricoid cartilage); leaves through the diaphragm's oesophageal opening at T10
options.B: Begins at C3; leaves through the diaphragm's aortic opening at T12
options.C: Begins at T1; leaves through the diaphragm's caval opening at T8
options.D: Begins at C6; leaves through the diaphragm's caval opening at T8

explanations.A: Correct. The oesophagus continues the pharynx from the level of the cricoid cartilage's lower border (C6), enters the thorax as the most posterior structure of the superior mediastinum, and, after crossing to the left in the posterior mediastinum, leaves the thorax through the diaphragm's own oesophageal opening at the T10 level, about an inch left of the midline. This is one of the diaphragm's three named openings, distinct from the more posterior and higher aortic opening (T12) and the more anterior, higher caval opening (T8). Pairing the oesophagus's C6 origin with its own T10 diaphragmatic opening, not the aortic or caval openings, is the discrimination this item tests.
explanations.B: Incorrect. C3 is too high for the oesophagus's origin, and the aortic opening at T12 belongs to the aorta and thoracic duct, not the oesophagus.
explanations.C: Incorrect. T1 is not the oesophagus's origin; it begins higher, at C6, continuing the pharynx, and the caval opening at T8 belongs to the inferior vena cava, not the oesophagus.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The origin at C6 is correct, but the oesophagus passes through its OWN oesophageal opening at T10, not through the caval opening at T8, which is reserved for the inferior vena cava.

questions.subject: gi
questions.learning_objective: State the vertebral levels at which the oesophagus begins and passes through the diaphragm.

questions.title: Diaphragmatic aortic opening: level and contents
questions.question: The aortic opening of the diaphragm lies at which vertebral level, and which structures pass through it besides the aorta?

options.A: T12; the azygos vein and thoracic duct
options.D: T12; the oesophagus and vagus nerves

explanations.A: Correct. The aortic opening, the lowest and most posterior of the diaphragm's three major openings, lies at the T12 level, strictly retro-diaphragmatic between the two crura, and transmits the aorta together with the azygos vein and the thoracic duct, both ascending from the abdomen alongside it. This is distinct from the oesophageal opening (T10, transmitting the oesophagus and vagus nerves) and the caval opening (T8, transmitting the inferior vena cava and right phrenic nerve). Pairing the aortic opening's T12 level with its own accompanying structures, the azygos vein and thoracic duct, rather than those of the other two openings, is the discrimination this item tests.
explanations.B: Incorrect. T10 is the oesophageal opening's level, which transmits the oesophagus and vagus nerves, not the aorta.
explanations.C: Incorrect. T8 is the caval opening's level, which transmits the inferior vena cava and right phrenic nerve, not the aorta.
explanations.D: Incorrect. T12 is the correct level for the aortic opening, but the oesophagus and vagus nerves pass through the separate oesophageal opening at T10, not through the aortic opening.

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: State the level of the diaphragm's aortic opening and the structures that accompany the aorta through it.

questions.title: Lobes and fissures of the right lung
questions.question: How many lobes does the right lung have, and which fissure is unique to it (absent from the left lung)?

options.A: Three lobes; the horizontal fissure, separating the upper and middle lobes
options.B: Two lobes; the oblique fissure, separating the upper and lower lobes
options.C: Three lobes; the oblique fissure, unique to the right lung
options.D: Two lobes; the horizontal fissure, separating the upper and lower lobes

explanations.A: Correct. The right lung has three lobes, upper, middle and lower, separated by two fissures: an oblique fissure, present in both lungs, and a horizontal fissure unique to the right lung, which splits off the middle lobe from the upper lobe. The left lung, by contrast, has only two lobes, upper and lower, divided by its own oblique fissure alone, with the lingula standing in as the left lung's small analogue of the right middle lobe rather than a separate lobe. Knowing that the horizontal fissure, not the oblique fissure which is present in both lungs, is the feature unique to the right lung is the discrimination this item tests.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Two lobes describes the left lung, not the right, which has three; and the oblique fissure is present in both lungs, not unique to either.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Three lobes is correct for the right lung, but the oblique fissure is present in both lungs, not a feature unique to the right.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The right lung has three lobes, not two, and its horizontal fissure separates the upper from the MIDDLE lobe, not the upper from the lower lobe.

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: State the number of lobes in the right lung and identify the horizontal fissure as unique to it.

questions.title: Diaphragmatic caval opening: level and companion nerve
questions.question: The caval opening of the diaphragm lies at which vertebral level, and which nerve accompanies the inferior vena cava through it?

explanations.A: Correct. The caval opening, the highest and most anterior of the diaphragm's three major openings, lies within the central tendon at the T8 level and transmits the inferior vena cava together with the right phrenic nerve, which accompanies it down onto the diaphragm's upper surface. This is distinct from the oesophageal opening (T10, oesophagus and vagus nerves) and the aortic opening (T12, aorta, azygos vein and thoracic duct). Pairing the caval opening's T8 level with the right, not left, phrenic nerve as its companion is the discrimination this item tests.
explanations.B: Incorrect. T10 is the oesophageal opening's level; and it is the RIGHT, not the left, phrenic nerve that accompanies the IVC through the caval opening.
explanations.C: Incorrect. T12 is the aortic opening's level, transmitting the aorta, azygos vein and thoracic duct, not the IVC or vagus nerves.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The splanchnic nerves pierce the diaphragm's crura separately, not through the caval opening, and are not the nerve that accompanies the IVC.

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: State the level of the diaphragm's caval opening and identify the right phrenic nerve as its companion structure.
